lessons.title: Read the brief
lessons.intro: Create a striking print advert for FLUX 01, a fictional trainer. Your job is to communicate movement, individuality and confidence through your design—not to recreate a real sports brand.
lessons.imageAlt: Finished FLUX trainer advert used as an example, not a design students must copy

steps.title: Choose an audience
steps.text: Write one sentence naming your intended audience and what visual style would appeal to them. Avoid claiming that everyone in an age group likes the same thing.

steps.title: Define your message
steps.text: Use MAKE YOUR MOVE as the starting headline, or write your own short alternative. Decide what you want the viewer to notice first, second and third.

steps.title: Plan the essentials
steps.text: Include a product image, a brand name, a headline and a clear call to action. Use FLUX 01 as the model name. The brand and product are fictional classroom assets; do not invent factual performance claims.

steps.title: Sketch two possibilities
steps.text: Try different product angles, headline positions and amounts of empty space. Choose one direction and explain why it suits your audience.

lessons.check: You can explain your audience, intended message and first visual focal point.
lessons.pitfall: A visually busy page is not automatically a powerful advert. Make one element lead.
lessons.challenge: Change the audience and sketch how your palette, typography and composition would need to change.
lessons.reason: A clear intention gives you a reason for each editing decision and something specific to evaluate afterwards.

lessons.title: Set up the document
lessons.intro: Start with a predictable print canvas. Getting the dimensions right now makes the rest of the composition easier.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft New Document dialog showing A4 portrait dimensions and 300 ppi

steps.title: Start a new project
steps.text: From PhotoCraft Home, choose A4 portrait under Start with a canvas. You can also choose New project and select the Classroom preset.

steps.title: Check dimensions and resolution
steps.text: Use 2480 × 3508 pixels, portrait orientation, with 300 pixels/inch resolution. If dimensions show inches, change the units to Pixels to inspect the pixel size.

steps.title: Keep the colour setup simple
steps.text: Use RGB colour, 8 bit and a white background for this lesson. Name the project FLUX advert – your name, then choose Create.

steps.title: Understand the numbers
steps.text: Pixels describe the actual image dimensions. PPI describes how tightly those pixels are placed when printed. Changing a PPI label does not create extra detail in a small source photograph.

lessons.check: The document status shows 2480 × 3508 px and 300 ppi.
lessons.pitfall: Do not enter 210 × 297 while the units are Pixels. Those are A4 dimensions in millimetres, not pixels.
lessons.challenge: Explain why a social-media square and an A4 print advert need different document dimensions.
lessons.reason: A deliberate format helps you design for the place your audience will actually see the advert.

lessons.title: Set rulers and alignment guides
lessons.intro: Give the advert a clear structure before adding the artwork. Rulers and non-printing guides help you keep margins and line up elements consistently.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft rulers and alignment guides around the advert canvas

steps.title: Show the rulers
steps.text: Choose View → Rulers. The scales along the top and left let you judge position and spacing. Keep the document dimensions in mind: this A4 canvas is 2480 × 3508 pixels.

steps.title: Create a consistent margin
steps.text: Choose View → Guides → New Guide Layout… to set up a margin or column structure. For a single guide, use View → Guides → New Guide… and choose its direction and position. You can also drag a guide from a ruler. Use guides to plan clear space around the headline, brand and call to action.

steps.title: Use snapping deliberately
steps.text: Enable View → Snap and View → Snap To → Guides when you want an element to align with a guide. If snapping pulls an element away from an intentional position, turn it off and judge the placement yourself.

steps.title: Preview without the construction lines
steps.text: Use View → Show → Guides to hide or reveal the guides while judging the composition. Guides are alignment aids, not part of the artwork; they do not appear in the exported advert. Hide them for an uncluttered final preview.

lessons.check: Rulers are visible, the canvas has a deliberate margin or guide structure, and you can hide the guides without changing the artwork.
lessons.pitfall: A guide is not a drawn line. If you need a visible line in the final advert, create artwork on a layer instead of relying on a ruler guide.
lessons.challenge: Compare a centred layout with a shared left-edge alignment. Use guides to build both, then explain which better supports your intended hierarchy.
lessons.reason: Consistent alignment and spacing make a bold advert feel controlled rather than accidentally crowded.

lessons.title: Place the practice assets
lessons.intro: Build the advert from separate files. Place Embedded adds an asset to the current document, rather than opening an unrelated new document.
lessons.imageAlt: A trainer image being placed as its own layer in PhotoCraft

steps.title: Download the practice pack
steps.text: Use the download button in this guide and extract the ZIP. Keep the original files in a project folder so you can locate them again.

steps.title: Place a background
steps.text: Choose File → Place Embedded… and select background-grid.png. Fit it to the page and confirm the transform with the tick. Keep it above the original Background layer.

steps.title: Place the trainer
steps.text: Choose File → Place Embedded… again and select trainer-original.png. Confirm the placement. The layer appears separately from the background.

steps.title: Keep the source editable
steps.text: A placed image is a Smart Object. Keep that editable version while scaling and arranging it; do not rasterise simply to move or resize it.

lessons.check: The background and trainer appear as separate entries in Layers.
lessons.pitfall: File → Open opens a document. File → Place Embedded adds an image inside the document you are already designing.
lessons.challenge: Compare placing an image with opening it as a new document. Explain when each approach is useful.
lessons.reason: Separate, editable source assets give you more freedom to revise the composition.

lessons.title: Move, scale and rotate
lessons.intro: Make the trainer feel like the hero of the advert. Use size, angle and position deliberately rather than dragging until something looks busy.
lessons.imageAlt: Move tool options with Auto-Select and Show Transform Controls in PhotoCraft

steps.title: Select the Move tool
steps.text: Choose the arrow/cross Move tool, or press V when you are not editing text.

steps.title: Try Auto-Select
steps.text: With Auto-Select enabled and set to Layer, clicking visible artwork can select its layer. Turn it off when overlapping artwork makes it hard to choose the intended layer; select that layer directly in Layers instead.

steps.title: Show the handles
steps.text: Enable Show Transform Controls. Select the trainer and use its transform handles to change size. Keep the width/height link enabled so the trainer stays in proportion.

steps.title: Compose with intention
steps.text: Try a strong diagonal angle and a large product image. Leave readable space for your headline. Confirm the transform with the tick when you are happy.

lessons.check: You can select the trainer, move it and resize it without stretching its proportions.
lessons.pitfall: If the wrong object moves, check the selected layer and Auto-Select before undoing or dragging again.
lessons.challenge: Make two compositions using the same assets. Compare how scale and diagonal direction change the sense of movement.
lessons.reason: Scale and placement create visual emphasis before the viewer reads a single word.

lessons.title: Organise the layers
lessons.intro: A good advert file should be understandable when you return to it later. Treat the Layers panel as a visual plan of the composition.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft Layers panel showing separately named advert elements

steps.title: Read the stack
steps.text: Layers higher in the list appear in front of lower layers where their visible pixels overlap. A full-page background near the top can hide your entire design.

steps.title: Rename as you go
steps.text: Double-click a layer name and use a clear label, such as Trainer, Headline, Streaks, Badge and Background graphic. Avoid renaming the wrong layer thumbnail.

steps.title: Reorder and compare
steps.text: Drag a layer up or down the stack. Use its eye icon to hide it temporarily and judge what that element contributes.

steps.title: Protect your foundation
steps.text: Once the background is positioned, lock it if you keep selecting or moving it accidentally. Keep the trainer and text separately editable.

lessons.check: You can identify each important element from its layer name and explain the order of the stack.
lessons.pitfall: Hiding a layer is different from deleting it. Use the eye icon when you want to compare versions safely.
lessons.challenge: Put part of the trainer in front of a headline and explain how that overlap creates depth without harming legibility.
lessons.reason: An organised layer stack supports experimentation and makes a complex image easier to refine.

lessons.title: Copy an asset into the advert
lessons.intro: Use both file-based placement and clipboard-based placement. This chapter uses the supplied badge so you practise a second way of bringing an image into your work.
lessons.imageAlt: A copied graphic placed as one image layer in PhotoCraft

steps.title: Copy the badge
steps.text: Choose Copy image on the badge asset card below. If the browser blocks this, right-click the full-size badge image and choose Copy image—not Copy image address.

steps.title: Focus the editor
steps.text: Return to PhotoCraft, click inside the editor, then press Ctrl+V. The image should appear as one placed layer. Confirm its placement with the tick.

steps.title: Position it deliberately
steps.text: Use the Move tool to place the badge where it supports the composition. Make it smaller than the main headline so it does not compete for first attention.

steps.title: Know the fallback
steps.text: If clipboard permissions are restricted, download flux-badge.png and use File → Place Embedded instead. Copying a web address provides text, not the image itself.

lessons.check: One paste has created one badge layer. You can move it independently.
lessons.pitfall: Clicking a browser tab's address bar and pasting there does not paste into PhotoCraft. Click the editor first.
lessons.challenge: Explain which workflow you would choose for an original photograph: a downloaded source file or a copied web image, and why.
lessons.reason: Knowing both routes helps you work reliably across different browser and school settings.

lessons.title: Remove the trainer's background
lessons.intro: Separate the trainer from its studio background so it can sit convincingly over your own design. Keep an editable mask rather than treating the cut-out as a finished result you cannot revisit.
lessons.imageAlt: Trainer cut-out with a layer mask after PhotoCraft background removal
lessons.videoNote: Processing wait shortened in this clip; the actual wait depends on your computer. Do not edit the document while removal runs.

steps.title: Choose the correct layer
steps.text: Select the Trainer image layer in Layers. Make sure you are not selecting the full-page background, a text layer or an unrelated graphic.

steps.title: Run the remover
steps.text: Choose Select → Remove Background. PhotoCraft applies a pending transform first. On first use, it downloads the AI model; let it finish. Processing then runs on this device.

steps.title: Inspect the mask
steps.text: The trainer layer should gain a black-and-white mask thumbnail. Your background graphic should show around the trainer, without an extra duplicate image layer.

steps.title: Judge the edge
steps.text: Zoom in around the sole, laces and gaps. Keep the result only if it is suitable for your advert. Undo restores the previous state; complex edges may need further mask refinement.

lessons.check: The studio backdrop is gone, the trainer remains on its own layer and the mask thumbnail is visible.
lessons.pitfall: Do not move, paste or edit the document while removal is running. A document-change warning protects your work from an outdated mask result.
lessons.challenge: Compare the cut-out over a light and a dark background. Which reveals edge problems most clearly?
lessons.reason: A convincing cut-out helps multiple source images feel like one designed composition.

lessons.title: Build the headline
lessons.intro: Let type carry the message. Use a small, deliberate type system rather than a different decorative font for every line.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft Type tool and a bold MAKE YOUR MOVE headline

steps.title: Add editable text
steps.text: Choose the Type tool, then click on the canvas. Replace the selected placeholder with MAKE YOUR MOVE. Confirm with the tick when finished.

steps.title: Choose a clear pairing
steps.text: Try Bebas Neue for the main headline and Inter for smaller information. These are already available in PhotoCraft. Start with one display family and one supporting family.

steps.title: Control scale and line breaks
steps.text: Make the headline large enough to read quickly. Try MAKE / YOUR / MOVE on separate lines. Adjust the size and position instead of stretching the letter shapes out of proportion.

steps.title: Add the supporting message
steps.text: Use separate text layers for FLUX 01, a short descriptive line and a call to action such as FIND YOUR NEXT MOVE. Keep them clearly smaller than the headline.

lessons.check: The headline is readable at a zoomed-out view, with supporting information in a clear second level.
lessons.pitfall: Pressing V while editing text types a letter. Confirm the text first, then use the Move tool shortcut.
lessons.challenge: Create a second typography version. Compare its character, readability and suitability for your intended audience.
lessons.reason: Typeface, size, spacing and contrast communicate a brand's character as well as its words.

lessons.title: Give the advert a clear hierarchy
lessons.intro: Step back from the tools and judge the design. Your viewer should understand where to look without being told.
lessons.imageAlt: Advert composition showing headline, trainer and smaller call to action

steps.title: Set a reading order
steps.text: Decide whether the headline or trainer is noticed first. Use size, contrast and position to support that choice. The brand and call to action should still be easy to find.

steps.title: Align with purpose
steps.text: Give text blocks a shared edge or a consistent relationship to the page. Leave a generous margin so important content does not feel accidentally cropped.

steps.title: Use empty space
steps.text: Avoid filling every gap. Give the headline and product enough clear space to remain distinct from the background graphics.

steps.title: Test at a distance
steps.text: Zoom out or ask a partner to view the advert briefly. Ask what they noticed first and what the advert is promoting—before explaining your intention.

lessons.check: A partner can identify the product, main message and next action quickly.
lessons.pitfall: A bright colour is not enough contrast if the background is equally bright and detailed. Judge the actual relationship between elements.
lessons.challenge: Remove one element from the advert. Does the message become clearer? Explain your decision.
lessons.reason: Hierarchy turns a collection of editing techniques into an effective piece of communication.

lessons.title: Blend the graphics into the design
lessons.intro: A layer's blend mode changes how its colours interact with layers beneath it. Test the effect on the actual artwork rather than choosing a mode just because its name sounds dramatic.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft blend-mode dropdown showing a graphic layer blended into an advert

steps.title: Add the streaks
steps.text: Place energy-streaks.png as a separate layer. Its black backdrop is intentional. Position it behind or beside the trainer so it suggests movement.

steps.title: Try Screen
steps.text: With Streaks selected, change the Normal dropdown at the top of Layers to Screen. Black contributes little to a Screen result, allowing bright streaks to combine with the design underneath.

steps.title: Try Multiply on the badge
steps.text: Select the dark badge on its white backdrop and try Multiply. White contributes little to a Multiply result while dark marks remain. This is different from making a true transparency mask.

steps.title: Reduce the intensity
steps.text: Adjust layer opacity if the effect competes with the product or text. Toggle the layer's eye icon to compare before and after.

lessons.check: You can explain why Screen suits the light-on-black streaks and Multiply suits a dark-on-white graphic.
lessons.pitfall: Blend modes affect the whole selected layer. Do not change the trainer's blend mode by accident when you mean to blend the streaks.
lessons.challenge: Compare Normal, Screen and Multiply on the same asset. Record what changes and choose the mode that supports your intention.
lessons.reason: Blending can integrate source graphics and add energy without piling opaque rectangles over your composition.

lessons.title: Use blending options sparingly
lessons.intro: Layer styles can help a product or headline separate from the background. They should support the design, rather than becoming its main attraction.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft Blending Options dialog used to apply a controlled layer effect

steps.title: Open Blending Options
steps.text: Select the intended layer, then choose Layer → Layer Style → Blending Options…. This is the layer-style dialog, not the blend-mode dropdown from the previous chapter.

steps.title: Test a subtle shadow
steps.text: Try Drop Shadow on the trainer or headline. Adjust opacity, distance and size while looking at the actual result. A small, soft shadow can create separation; a heavy halo can make the image less convincing.

steps.title: Test a stroke where useful
steps.text: A restrained Stroke can help type hold its edge against a busy area. Compare it with moving the text to a clearer part of the page—an effect is not always the best solution.

steps.title: Keep only what helps
steps.text: Compare the design with the effect enabled and disabled, then confirm the dialog. Use a consistent visual logic rather than different lighting directions on every element.

lessons.check: You can point to a specific readability or depth problem that your chosen effect improves.
lessons.pitfall: Blending Options and a layer's blend mode are related editing controls, but they are not interchangeable tools.
lessons.challenge: Solve the same readability problem twice: once with a layer style and once using composition alone. Evaluate which solution is stronger.
lessons.reason: Restraint makes a professional finish more convincing than applying every available effect.

lessons.title: Experiment with History
lessons.intro: Use History to investigate changes and recover from mistakes, while keeping proper saved versions of important stages.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft History panel listing recent advert edits

steps.title: Find the panel
steps.text: History appears above Layers in the classroom workspace. If it is hidden, open it from the Window menu.

steps.title: Make one controlled change
steps.text: Move an element or change an effect. Identify the matching new entry in History.

steps.title: Step back and compare
steps.text: Use Ctrl+Z to undo, or select an earlier History state. Compare the result carefully. Moving back then making a fresh edit can replace the later branch of changes.

steps.title: Save meaningful versions
steps.text: Keep separate downloaded project versions before major changes, such as flux-layout-v1.pcraft and flux-refined-v2.pcraft. History is not a replacement for saving or recovery.

lessons.check: You can undo an intentional test edit and recognise the corresponding state in History.
lessons.pitfall: Browser crashes, reloads and profile cleanup can affect session history. Keep downloaded editable project files.
lessons.challenge: Capture two stages of your design and explain a specific improvement, rather than saying only that the final version looks better.
lessons.reason: A documented editing process shows how experimentation informed your decisions.

lessons.title: Save the project and export the advert
lessons.intro: Keep an editable master as well as a finished image. These files do different jobs.
lessons.imageAlt: PhotoCraft export workflow for a finished advert

steps.title: Download an editable project
steps.text: Use File → Save As… and keep a .pcraft project. This preserves your editable document for later work. Check the actual download location on your school computer.

steps.title: Export a finished image
steps.text: Use File → Export → Export As… and choose PNG or JPEG. Check that you export the complete document at the intended size, not just a selected layer.

steps.title: Choose the right format
steps.text: PNG is useful for crisp graphics and supports transparency. JPEG is useful for a smaller photographic image but does not retain transparency. Neither is a replacement for the editable project.

steps.title: Inspect the download
steps.text: Open the exported file. Check the full composition, spelling, edges, contrast and cropping. Submit the files your teacher requests and keep the original assets with your project.

lessons.check: You have both an editable .pcraft file and a finished PNG or JPEG that opens correctly.
lessons.pitfall: A downloaded export is a flattened deliverable. Opening it again will not restore the separate text and image layers from your project.
lessons.challenge: Compare a PNG and JPEG export at a similar viewing size. Look for file-size and image-quality differences before choosing a submission format.
lessons.reason: Choosing and checking the output is part of the design process, not an administrative afterthought.

lessons.title: Review, explain and make it yours
lessons.intro: The example is a starting point, not a target to trace. Your final advert should show your own purposeful decisions.
lessons.imageAlt: Example finished FLUX advert for comparison and evaluation

steps.title: Evaluate communication
steps.text: Explain what the advert communicates, who it is for and how the main image, typography and palette support that intention. Refer to specific visual evidence.

steps.title: Evaluate technique
steps.text: Inspect the cut-out edge, transforms, type, alignment and effects. Name a technical problem you solved and how your method changed the result.

steps.title: Show development
steps.text: Keep a sketch, an earlier screenshot and the finished outcome. Explain one decision you changed after testing or feedback.

steps.title: Credit and extend
steps.text: Record the source of the supplied practice assets and any extra material you add. Label AI-generated practice imagery honestly. Build an original variation through a different audience, layout, copy or palette—not by copying a real brand's campaign.

lessons.check: Your evaluation links intention, visual choices, technical decisions and evidence of development.
lessons.pitfall: Listing the tools you used is not the same as explaining why those tools improved the advert.
lessons.challenge: Adapt your advert for a square digital format while preserving its hierarchy. Explain what you moved, removed or changed.
lessons.reason: A convincing outcome and a thoughtful explanation of your process strengthen each other.
